transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess the short version is I can’t seem to slow myself down since I stopped working. I’m 65 now, and not going off to a job anymore, but my body still acts like I’ve got a work crew waiting on me or a schedule I’m supposed to keep.

I’m up and moving most of the day, going from one little job to the next—fix this, straighten that, check something, start something else. It’s not even always important stuff. It’s just like I don’t know how to sit still and be retired, if that makes sense. I thought stopping work would mean I’d relax more, but instead I’m kind of pacing through the day looking for the next thing to do. That’s really what brought me in.
Do you get upsetting thoughts that keep popping into your mind and make you feel like you have to keep busy or check things?

I don’t think so… not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think. I mean, I do get thoughts like, “Oh, I should go take care of that,” or “I better not forget to look at that thing in the garage,” but it doesn’t feel like some awful thought that scares me or makes me check something over and over.

It’s more like my mind just keeps throwing tasks at me, if that makes sense. One thing reminds me of another thing, and then I’m up doing it before I’ve really decided whether it needs doing. But I wouldn’t say I’m having upsetting thoughts popping in that force me to keep busy. At least I haven’t noticed it that way.
Have there ever been times when you felt unusually energized and needed much less sleep than usual without feeling tired?

I’m not sure I’d say that, no. I mean, I’ve had plenty of times where I’m up early and I get moving right away, and my wife would probably say I act like I’ve already had three cups of coffee before breakfast. But needing much less sleep and not feeling tired… I don’t think so, not in some unusual way.

At my age, sleep is kind of up and down anyway, you know? Some nights I wake up, or I’m thinking about what I want to do the next day, but if I don’t sleep enough, I usually feel it. I might still get up and start doing things, because that’s just how I tend to be, but I wouldn’t say I’m running on no sleep and feeling great. It’s more that I have a hard time settling, not that I suddenly don’t need sleep.
Have you been this way—always on the go and jumping from one task to another—since you were young?

Yes… I think so. I mean, looking back, it wasn’t something we had a name for when I was a kid, but I was always kind of like this.

Even in grade school, teachers would say I was bright, but scattered. That was the word, or something like it. I’d lose pencils constantly, forget where I put papers, that sort of thing. And I remember getting in trouble for calling out answers before I was supposed to—like I knew the answer and it just came out before I raised my hand.

They were always reminding me to finish my work before recess, too. I’d start it, then get sidetracked or be looking around or messing with something at my desk, and then suddenly everyone else was done and I still had half a page left. So yes, I’d say it goes way back. It’s not just a retirement thing, even though being retired has made it more noticeable.
Do you still get easily distracted when you’re trying to focus on one thing?

Yes, I do. Even when I’m trying to do something I actually want to do, like painting, I can be right in the middle of figuring out a color or a line, and then a truck goes by outside or I hear something in the yard, and my mind just sort of jumps over there. Then I’ll realize I’ve lost the thread of what I was doing.

Same with planning out a story or an idea. I’ll sit down thinking, “Okay, I’m going to work this out,” and then I’ll remember something in the garden, or wonder if I left a tool out there, and suddenly I’m not with the story anymore. It’s not always a big dramatic thing, but it happens pretty easily. Once my attention gets pulled away, it can take me a while to get back to where I was.
Has being this distractible and always on the go caused problems for you in your work, relationships, or handling everyday responsibilities?

Yes, it has. I mean, I wouldn’t say my whole life has fallen apart because of it or anything, but it causes problems—mostly the kind that add up and make other people frustrated with me.

My wife, for one, has basically had to take over the calendar. If there’s an appointment, a family thing, something I said I’d do, she’ll write it down and remind me, and sometimes remind me again. She also checks behind me more than I’d like to admit—like, “Did you call so-and-so?” or “Did you bring that form?” And I get a little embarrassed because I’m a grown man, you know? I don’t want her to have to manage me that way, but if she doesn’t, things slip.

And outside the house, yes, I’ve had to apologize more than once. At the community center, or with the garden group, I’ll say I’m going to help with something or bring something or show up at a certain time, and then I get pulled into something else or lose track, and suddenly I’ve let people down. I don’t mean to. I really don’t. But meaning well doesn’t fix it when somebody was counting on me.
